Magnificent dialectic: A dualism is possible only because the two partners who make up the pair are, at bottom, in agreement about something. For that very reason, the dualism ought to end in unity—if there were really nothing else on earth except this spiritual unity which, in order to sustain the opposition, requires the Iron Curtain. But the underlying unity does not exhaust the unity of the world.

It would be terrible. It would be a disaster, a horror. It would mean the simultaneous end of spirit, life, and soul if the underlying unity shared by these two parties actually resulted in a real unity.
They are two opposing sides facing each other within the same ideological world.
The common idea they share is the secret behind their division into two.
The moment this common element is recognized, the duality falls apart.
The opposition between their economic systems is only an antithetical development—two opposing applications—of the same underlying idea: a philosophy of history.
It follows that neither of these two sides in the present division of the world will be the one that creates world unity.

Think about it for a moment.
Something just as simple as <…> follows:
Anyone who is not extraordinarily likeable to me is not a human being. Whether he is an inhuman being or a subhuman being is a separate question.
It is, after all, a perfectly constructed humanitarian syllogism:
Every human being is good and noble.
Carl Schmitt is not good and noble.
Therefore Carl Schmitt is not a human being.
This, gentlemen, is the essence of present-day humanism.
What we are dealing with, then, is discrimination and criminalization.
